# MCP Overview

This page is for Developer.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI agents, such as Claude, Cursor, and ChatGPT, discover and call tools. An MCP server publishes a list of tools, each with a name, a description, and an input schema. The agent picks the right tool for a request and calls it, instead of scraping pages or calling raw APIs.

BigCommerce supports MCP in three ways. Each one serves a different kind of agent and acts with a different level of access.

Capability  | Who it’s for  | Acts as  | Availability
--- | --- | --- | ---
Storefront MCP  | Shopping agents and chat widgets that connect to your storefront  | A shopper: a guest, a logged-in customer, or a B2B buyer  | Generally available
WebMCP  | AI agents running inside a shopper’s browser  | The shopper, in their own browser session  | On by default for eligible storefronts
Store Management MCP  | Store administrators who use an agent to run their store  | A control panel user, limited to the scopes granted to them  | Early access

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI agents, such as Claude, Cursor, and ChatGPT, discover and call tools. The agent picks the right tool for a request and calls it, instead of scraping pages or calling raw APIs. BigCommerce supports MCP in three ways. Capability Who it’s for Acts as Availability Storefront MCP Shopping agents and chat widgets that connect to your storefront A shopper: a guest, a logged-in customer, or a B2B buyer Generally available WebMCP AI agents running inside a shopper’s browser The shopper, in their own browser session On by default for eligible storefronts Store Management MCP Store administrators who use an agent to run their store A control panel user, limited to the scopes granted to them Early access The Docs MCP server is separate from these capabilities. It lets your AI tool search the BigCommerce developer documentation, and it can’t read or change store data. Use cases Storefront MCP Use Storefront MCP to let an agent shop your catalog for someone: a conversational shopping assistant, a chat widget on your storefront, or a third-party AI shopping app. The agent can search products, compare options, build a cart, and hand the shopper a checkout link. Every store gets the storefront tools. Catalog, cart, and checkout tools work for guests, logged-in customers, and B2B buyers. B2B Edition stores get extra tools. Authenticated buyers can also manage shopping lists and request and work with quotes. Shopper context carries over. On Stencil storefronts, session sync links the agent to the shopper’s existing browser session, so the agent sees their login, cart, and pricing. For tools and setup, see Storefront MCP . WebMCP Use WebMCP to make your storefront work well with AI assistants that shoppers already use in their browser. Instead of guessing their way around your pages, those agents call your store’s shopping tools directly, and the shopper completes checkout on your site. You don’t need to change your theme or write code. For how it works and how to verify it, see WebMCP . Store Management MCP Use Store Management MCP to let an administrator work on the store through an agent: look up and update products and prices, set inventory levels, create promotions, look up and refund orders, and read store details. For tools, client setup, and limitations, see Store Management MCP . Enablement and permissions You manage all three capabilities in the control panel under Settings → API and MCP → MCP . Each one has its own card on that page. Storefront MCP Who can enable it: The store owner turns on Storefront MCP and accepts the terms of service. Connection: Each storefront gets its own MCP server URL. Agents connect to that URL directly. No API account or admin credentials are involved. What agents can access: Only what a shopper can access on that storefront. Guests get the storefront tools. Logged-in customers and B2B buyers connect through session sync , and each B2B tool is available only to buyers who hold the matching Buyer Portal permission. For steps, see Enable Storefront MCP . WebMCP Who can enable it: Nobody has to. WebMCP is on by default for Stencil storefronts and for Catalyst storefronts hosted on Cloudflare. Custom headless storefronts on Cloudflare can request it from BigCommerce Support . Which tools it exposes: Two image scanning tools by default. When Storefront MCP is on, its shopping tools are synced to WebMCP automatically, so you manage one set of tools. What agents can access: The same prices, cart, and session the shopper sees in their browser. Tool calls go from the shopper’s browser to your storefront’s own domain. Opting out: Turn off the WebMCP toggle. See Opt out of WebMCP . Store Management MCP Access: Store Management MCP is in early access and available to all stores. Who can enable it: Only the store owner can turn on Management MCP and accept the terms of service. Connection: Agents connect to https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp , sign in through the standard BigCommerce login (OAuth 2.1 with PKCE), and then the user chooses which store to connect. To connect to one specific store, agents can use https://api.bigcommerce.com/stores/{store_hash}/mcp instead. The agent never receives a password or API token. What agents can access: Every user starts with no access. An administrator grants scopes per user, one area at a time (for example, Products, Inventory, Orders, or Promotions), at None, read-only, or modify. An agent only sees the tools within the connecting user’s scopes. Delegating: The store owner can let other users view or assign scopes with the View AI MCP Scopes Grants and Create AI MCP Scopes Grants permissions. Store Management MCP scopes apply to the user, not to a specific agent, and each scope covers its whole area. Grant modify only where the user should be able to change data. For example, Orders modify lets an agent refund orders. For steps, see Store Management MCP .

pages.title: Store Management MCP | BigCommerce Docs (https://docs.bigcommerce.com/developer/api-reference/mcp/store-management)
pages.text: Store Management MCP | BigCommerce Docs For AI agents: a documentation index is available at the root level at /llms.txt. Append /llms.txt to any URL for a page-level index, or .md for the markdown version of any page. Skip to navigation On this page Before you begin Enable Store Management MCP for your store Grant a user access to connect an agent Delegate scope management Connect your MCP client Server address Authentication Connect a client Rate limits Available tools Tool details update_product_content set_product_custom_fields get_orders get_refund_quote create_refund get_promotions create_promotion get_store_info Example prompts Troubleshooting Early access limitations Share feedback Get help Scroll to top This page is for Developer. Store Management MCP lets an AI agent — Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, or any other Model Context Protocol (MCP)-compatible client — work directly with your BigCommerce store’s catalog, pricing, inventory, orders, promotions, and store profile. This guide covers how an administrator turns on access, how to connect a client, and how to use the tools available in early access. Before you begin Your store must be active. Suspended, cancelled, or closed stores can’t connect. An administrator must turn on Store Management MCP for the store (see Enable Store Management MCP ) and grant scopes to the specific user who will connect an agent (see Grant a user access ). Every user starts with no access. If you manage more than one store, repeat both steps separately in each store. A grant in one store doesn’t carry over to another. Enable Store Management MCP for your store Only the store owner can turn on Store Management MCP — this step can’t be delegated to another user. In the control panel, go to Settings → API and MCP → MCP . You can also search for “MCP” from the Settings page. Turn on the Management MCP toggle. Select Accept terms and join beta to accept the terms of service for the Management MCP server and tools for AI agents. This is a binding acknowledgment on behalf of your organization. Once accepted, the page records who accepted the terms and when, and reveals the MCP API Endpoint to connect your agent to (see Server address ) and a Manage AI agent access button. Turning Management MCP off revokes access for every connected agent, though it can take a few minutes to take effect everywhere — see Early access limitations . Grant a user access to connect an agent From the Management MCP card, select Manage AI agent access , then Assign agent access . Pick an existing control panel user and set their access, one scope at a time: Scope Levels Notes Products None, read-only, modify Backs viewing, searching, creating, and categorizing products, editing existing product text and custom fields, and updating catalog and price-list pricing (modify required for editing and pricing) Inventory None, read-only, modify Backs viewing and setting inventory levels Promotions None, read-only, modify Read-only unlocks get_promotions . Modify also unlocks create_promotion Store None, read-only Unlocks get_store_info , which returns your store’s business contact details Customers None, read-only No tool uses this scope yet — granting it has no effect today Orders None, read-only, modify Read-only unlocks get_orders , which returns order summaries without shopper contact details. Modify also unlocks get_refund_quote and create_refund , which can refund orders Selecting modify implicitly includes read access. Only grant Orders modify if you want your agent to be able to refund orders. A refund returns real money to a shopper and can’t be undone through the tool. Promotions modify lets your agent create discounts, which are always created disabled until someone enables them in the control panel. None of the tools return shopper names, email addresses, phone numbers, or addresses. The Store scope returns your business’s contact information, not shopper data. However, if your store is registered to a home address, or uses a personal email or phone number, granting Store access lets your agent see those details. Three details about how grants work: Every new user starts at None across every scope. Connecting an agent as that user grants it nothing until you explicitly assign scopes. Grants are flat, not per-agent. If a user connects both Claude and ChatGPT, both get exactly the same access — there’s no way yet to give two agents different scopes for the same person. Grants are per store. A user who administers several stores needs scopes assigned separately in each one. The AI agent access page lists every user you’ve granted access to, with their scopes spelled out in plain text and Edit and Clear links next to each. Clearing a grant stops future tool calls for that user, though an already-connected session can continue until it expires — see Early access limitations . Delegate scope management By default, only the store owner can view or assign AI agent access. To let another team member manage it, go to Settings → Users , edit their permissions, and grant one or both of these System Admin Permissions: Permission Lets that user View AI MCP Scopes Grants View the AI agent access page and see who has what access Create AI MCP Scopes Grants Assign or edit which scopes a user’s agent can use This only delegates scope management. Turning Management MCP on or off for the store, in the section above, remains store owner-only. Connect your MCP client The following clients were tested during this phase. In every case, you point the client at the Store Management MCP address and sign in through the BigCommerce login — you never paste a password, API key, or token into the client. Any client with standard MCP and OAuth support should work, even if it isn’t listed here. Menu names in third-party clients change often. If a step doesn’t match what you see, check that client’s MCP documentation. Server address Connect your MCP client to this address: https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp The same address works for every store. After you sign in with your BigCommerce login, you choose which store to connect. This is the address the MCP API Endpoint field on the Management MCP card shows. To connect to one specific store, use its per-store address instead: https://api.bigcommerce.com/stores/{store_hash}/mcp To copy a store’s per-store address, expand Working with multiple stores? on the Management MCP card. The Store-specific MCP API Endpoint field shows it. Add it as a separate custom connector for each store. Because the per-store address already identifies the store, the connection flow has no separate store picker. If your BigCommerce user doesn’t have access to that store, sign-in fails. Authentication Connections use OAuth 2.1 with PKCE. Your MCP client registers itself automatically, so there’s no client ID or client secret to create or manage. When you connect, your client sends you to the standard BigCommerce login. Your agent never sees or holds your BigCommerce password, session, or any other credential. If your login normally uses two-factor authentication or single sign-on, it works the same way here. The scopes assigned to your BigCommerce user (see Grant a user access ) determine which tools your agent can see after you sign in. Every tool call is checked against those scopes on the server, on every request — nothing your agent sends is trusted to establish its identity or permissions. Connect a client The following steps use https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp . To connect to one specific store, use the per-store address https://api.bigcommerce.com/stores/{store_hash}/mcp in its place. Claude Desktop Claude (browser) Claude Code Cursor ChatGPT Grok Go to Settings → Connectors and select Add custom connector . Paste the server address: https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp Select Connect , then sign in with your BigCommerce login when prompted. To configure the connection manually instead, add an entry to the Claude Desktop config file that uses mcp-remote as a bridge: claude_desktop_config.json { " mcpServers " : { " bigcommerce " : { " command " : " npx " , " args " : [ " mcp-remote " , " https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp " ] } } } Rate limits Store Management MCP limits how many requests each user can send to each store. The allowance depends on the store’s plan. It applies to the user, not to the agent, so every agent a user connects to the same store shares one allowance. Both server addresses also share it, so switching between https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp and the per-store address doesn’t reset it. When a user goes over the allowance, the tool call fails. Your agent is told that the call was rate limited and how many seconds to wait before trying again, and the response includes a Retry-After header. Available tools Early access includes 16 tools across five scopes: Products, Inventory, Orders, Promotions, and Store. An agent only sees the tools within the scopes granted to the connecting user — tools outside those scopes aren’t just blocked, they’re invisible to the agent. Tool Scope Description get_product Products Returns a single product’s details, including variants, images, and custom fields. search_products Products Finds products by keyword, name, SKU, product ID, or category, one page of results at a time. Returns summaries only (no variants, images, custom fields, or descriptions); use get_product for full detail. create_product Products Creates a catalog product from a name, type, weight, and price, plus optional catalog fields. New products are always created hidden, so nothing an agent creates goes live until someone reviews and publishes it. assign_product_categories Products Adds, replaces, or removes a product’s category assignments, up to 100 categories per call. update_product_content Products (modify) Edits the text on an existing product: name, description, page title, meta description, search keywords, warranty, availability text, and pre-order message. set_product_custom_fields Products (modify) Adds or changes custom fields (name/value pairs such as “Material: Wool”) on an existing product. update_catalog_prices Products (modify) Sets price, sale price, cost price, MAP price, and retail price on up to 10 products and 50 variants per call. Omitting a field keeps its current value; sending an explicit null clears it. update_price_list_records Products (modify) Updates up to 1,000 price list records in one call, for stores that use price lists. Omitting a money field keeps its current value ( price can’t be cleared). Pricing tiers are replaced in full on each call. get_inventory_levels Inventory Returns per-location stock levels and a per-item total. Returns inventory data only — no product names, prices, or images. set_inventory_levels Inventory Sets on-hand stock for up to 2,000 items to an exact quantity. This is always an absolute set, never a relative adjustment. get_orders Orders Lists orders as summaries: status, dates, totals, payment method, and refunded amount. Never returns shopper names, email addresses, phone numbers, addresses, IP addresses, staff notes, or order comments. Can also return each order’s line items and shipping consignments, which the refund tools need. get_refund_quote Orders (modify) Calculates what refunding part or all of an order would pay out, including tax and rounding, and the payment options for paying it back. Moves no money and is safe to retry. create_refund Orders (modify) Refunds part or all of an order using one of the payment options from a quote. Moves money and can’t be undone through the tool. get_promotions Promotions Lists the store’s promotions, or reads one by ID. Can also find which promotion a coupon code belongs to. create_promotion Promotions (modify) Creates one promotion with one rule: a percentage or fixed amount off products or categories, a percentage off the order, or free shipping. New promotions are always created disabled, so nothing an agent creates discounts anything until someone reviews and enables it. get_store_info Store Reads the store’s profile: store name, contact email, phone, and address, either store-wide or as overridden on a specific channel. Tool details The following tools have behavior worth knowing before you use them. update_product_content Partial update. Only the fields your agent sends are changed; everything else keeps its current value. Sending an empty string clears that field. The product name can’t be cleared. Search keywords replace the whole list. Keywords are stored as one comma-separated string, so your agent has to read the current keywords first and send back the full set, not only the new word. Descriptions accept HTML or plain text, not Markdown. Markdown is stored as-is, so shoppers would see the raw asterisks. Text only. It can’t change prices, stock, visibility, categories, brand, SKU, weight, dimensions, images, variants, or option sets. Custom fields have their own tool, set_product_custom_fields . No undo. The previous text can’t be recovered through the tool, so have your agent confirm new wording with you before it writes. One product per call. It’s safe to retry. set_product_custom_fields Matched by exact, case-sensitive name. If a field with that name exists, its value is updated. Otherwise, a new field is added. “Material” and “material” are two different fields. Never deletes. Fields you don’t name are left alone. Custom fields can’t be removed through this tool, and an empty value is rejected. Not atomic. Each field is written separately, so if a call fails partway through, the fields before the failure are already saved. Your agent gets a result for each field: created, updated, or unchanged. Limits. Up to 50 fields per call, 250 characters per name or value, and 200 custom fields per product. It’s safe to retry. get_orders Summaries only. Each order includes status, dates, totals, payment method, payment status, and refunded amount. It never returns shopper names, email addresses, phone numbers, shipping or billing addresses, IP addresses, staff notes, or order comments. Line items on request. Your agent can ask for each order’s product lines and shipping consignments. The product line id is the order product ID, not the catalog product ID, and the shipping id identifies the shipping consignment. The refund tools need both, and no other tool returns them. Asking for line items lowers the maximum page size from 250 to 25. Truncated item lists are flagged. If an order has a consignment with more than 50 line items, the response says the list is incomplete. Your agent shouldn’t quote or refund from an incomplete list. Filters. Your agent can filter by customer ID ( 0 selects guest orders), customer email, status, channel, payment method, creation date, and archived state. get_refund_quote Moves no money. A quote only calculates the refund, so it’s safe to retry. It’s also the required first step before create_refund . Typed items. Each item to refund has a type. PRODUCT and GIFT_WRAPPING are refunded by quantity. SHIPPING , HANDLING , ORDER , and FEE are refunded by amount; use ORDER for a partial refund that isn’t tied to a product. Listing the same item twice is rejected. Payment options to choose from. The quote returns the total, including tax and rounding, and a list of options. Each option is a complete way to pay back the whole refund, and it can split the amount across the payment methods the order was paid with, for example part back to the card and part as store credit. Your agent should show you the options and let you choose, not pick one for you. One order per call. An archived order can still be quoted. Refunding an archived order hasn’t been verified, so have your agent check the order isn’t archived first. create_refund Moves money, with no undo. It returns the money to the shopper and debits your store. Have your agent confirm the total and the payment option with you before it calls the tool. Needs the quote’s numbers. Your agent sends the same items, one payment option copied exactly from the quote, and the quote’s total. Before submitting, the tool takes a fresh quote and refuses if the total or the payment option no longer matches. When that happens, no money moves, and your agent has to quote again and confirm with you again. Never retried. There’s no way to make a refund safe to repeat, so a second submit can refund the shopper twice. If a call fails and the outcome is unknown, your agent should check the order’s refunds in the control panel before doing anything else. When the error says no money moved, your agent can fix the request, take a fresh quote, and try again. Declined payments. A refund can be recorded even though one of its payment methods declined. The response lists every payment with whether it was declined, and your agent should tell you if any were. Reason. An optional reason of up to 1,000 characters is kept on the refund record. One order per call. The option to skip the store’s tax calculation isn’t available through the tool. get_promotions Read-only. It shows how promotions are set up (status, schedule, channels, customer groups, rules, and usage count), but not redemption history, revenue, or which customers used a promotion. Coupon codes aren’t returned. Your agent can look up the promotion a code belongs to, but it can’t list a promotion’s codes. No individual shoppers. Customer targeting is shown as group and segment IDs only. Empty channel list means every channel. A promotion with an empty channel list applies to every channel, not none. create_promotion Always created disabled. Status isn’t something your agent can set, so a new promotion discounts nothing until someone reviews it and enables it in the control panel. Four kinds. percentage_off_products and fixed_amount_off_products need at least one product ID or category ID. percentage_off_order takes a percentage and an optional minimum order amount. free_shipping takes an optional minimum order amount and optional shipping zone IDs, and applies to all zones when you omit them. One promotion, one rule. It can’t create buy-one-get-one offers, free gifts, tiered or stacked discounts, customer group or segment targeting, country targeting, day-of-week schedules, or any condition other than a minimum order amount. Create those in the control panel. Parameters must match the kind. A parameter the chosen kind doesn’t use is rejected instead of ignored. Coupon promotions have no code. Your agent can create a promotion that’s redeemed with a coupon, but not the code itself. Add the code in the control panel when you enable the promotion. Optional settings. Start and end dates (RFC 3339 timestamps with an offset, not bare dates), a total usage limit, whether the promotion can be used with other promotions (it can by default), and channel IDs. Without channel IDs, the promotion applies to every channel. Each ID list takes up to 50 unique IDs, and amounts are in the store’s default currency. Not safe to retry. Creating a promotion twice makes two promotions, and both apply to a cart. If a call fails and the outcome is unknown, your agent should check the store’s promotions before trying again. get_store_info Read-only. Returns store name, contact email, phone, address, and address type, plus any new store email that’s waiting for confirmation. Channel reads show overrides only. If your agent asks for a specific channel, a blank field means that channel uses the store-wide value, not that the field is empty. Business data, not shopper data. See the note under Grant a user access about stores registered to personal contact details. Example prompts The following prompts map directly onto the tools above: “Look up SKU WIDGET-100 and tell me its current price and stock level.” → get_product “Find all products with ‘scarf’ in the name.” → search_products “Create a hidden product called ‘Autumn Wool Scarf’, physical, 0.3 kg, $34.99, SKU SCARF-AUT-01.” → create_product “File that scarf product under the Winter and Accessories categories.” → assign_product_categories “Raise the price of SKUs WIDGET-100, WIDGET-101, and WIDGET-102 by 10%.” → get_product to confirm current prices, then update_catalog_prices to apply the change “Update the Wholesale price list so SKU MUG-042 is $6.50.” → update_price_list_records “What’s our current stock level on SKU MUG-042?” → get_inventory_levels “We just received 50 units of SKU MUG-042 — update the stock count.” → set_inventory_levels “Show me the last 10 orders.” → get_orders (only works if the connecting user has been granted the Orders scope) “How much would it cost to refund one unit of the Autumn Wool Scarf on order 180, and how could I pay it back?” → get_orders to find the order’s line items, then get_refund_quote “Refund that to the original card.” → create_refund , after your agent has shown you the quote and you’ve confirmed the total and payment option “Rewrite the description of product 123 to emphasize that it’s handmade, and show me the new text before you save it.” → get_product , then update_product_content “Add ‘eco-friendly’ to the search keywords on the Autumn Wool Scarf.” → get_product to read the current keywords, then update_product_content with the full list “Set Material to ‘100% Merino Wool’ and Care to ‘Hand wash cold’ on product 123.” → set_product_custom_fields “Which promotions are running right now on my US channel?” → get_promotions “Which promotion does the code SAVE20 belong to, and when does it end?” → get_promotions “Create a 15% off promotion on the Winter category.” → create_promotion , which creates it disabled for you to review “Set up free shipping on orders over $75.” → create_promotion “What email address and phone number are shoppers seeing for my store?” → get_store_info Your agent reports what it did, not what it verified. Spot-check a price or stock change against the control panel the first few times. Scopes aren’t field-level, so an agent with Products modify access can change any price it can see, not just the one you asked about — be specific about what you want changed. The same applies to refunds and promotions: check the amounts and payment options before you confirm. After you’ve tried a few prompts, share feedback on what worked and what didn’t. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause What to do Your agent doesn’t offer a tool you expect (for example, no pricing tool at all) The connecting user’s scope for that area is None, or set to read-only where modify is needed Check the user’s grant on the AI agent access page. A missing or insufficient scope makes the tool invisible, not blocked, so there’s no error to see. Connecting fails at login The store isn’t active, or Store Management MCP hasn’t been turned on Confirm the store’s status is active and that Enable Store Management MCP is complete Sign-in fails when you connect with a per-store address Your BigCommerce user doesn’t have access to the store in the address, or the store hash is wrong Check the store hash in the address, or connect to https://api.bigcommerce.com/mcp and choose the store after you sign in Your agent says a call was rate limited The connecting user went over their request allowance for this store Wait the number of seconds your agent reports, then try again. Connecting another agent or switching server addresses doesn’t help, because they share the same allowance. See Rate limits . A tool call is rejected after previously working A scope was changed or revoked since you connected, or your session expired Reconnect. Sessions are intentionally short-lived during this phase — see Early access limitations . A newly created product isn’t showing on your storefront Expected — create_product always creates hidden products Review and publish the product yourself from the control panel Your agent says it can’t add images, variants, or set visibility on a product it just created Expected — create_product only creates the base record Make those changes in the control panel Your agent can see products but can’t edit their text, custom fields, or prices The connecting user has Products set to read-only, and update_product_content , set_product_custom_fields , update_catalog_prices , and update_price_list_records need modify Change the user’s Products scope to modify on the AI agent access page Your agent doesn’t offer get_promotions or get_store_info The user’s Promotions or Store scope is still None Grant read-only for that scope on the AI agent access page A custom field your agent “updated” shows up twice The name didn’t match the existing field exactly (for example, different capitalization), so a new field was created Delete the extra field in the control panel, then ask again using the exact existing name Your agent says it can’t show coupon codes Expected — get_promotions doesn’t return coupon codes View codes in the control panel under Marketing → Promotions Your agent can look up orders but doesn’t offer the refund tools The connecting user has Orders set to read-only, and get_refund_quote and create_refund need modify Change the user’s Orders scope to modify on the AI agent access page. Your agent can see promotions but doesn’t offer create_promotion The connecting user has Promotions set to read-only, and create_promotion needs modify Change the user’s Promotions scope to modify on the AI agent access page A promotion your agent created isn’t discounting anything Expected — create_promotion always creates promotions disabled Review the promotion and enable it in the control panel under Marketing → Promotions A coupon promotion your agent created has no code Expected — create_promotion can’t create coupon codes Add the code in the control panel under Marketing → Promotions before you enable the promotion Your agent says a refund wasn’t sent because the quote no longer matches The order, its payments, or the refund total changed after the quote, or the payment option wasn’t copied exactly Ask your agent to take a fresh quote, show you the options, and confirm again. No money moved. A refund was recorded but one payment shows as declined The payment provider refused its part of the refund Check the order’s refunds in the control panel and resolve the declined part there. Don’t ask your agent to submit the refund again. Your agent reports that it doesn’t know whether a refund went through The request timed out or the store returned an error before confirming the refund Check the order’s refunds in the control panel before doing anything else. Submitting again can refund the shopper twice. You want to see which agents are actively connected, or force one to disconnect immediately There’s no self-service view of live connections yet Contact BigCommerce support Early access limitations No shopper personal data. None of the tools return shopper names, email addresses, phone numbers, or addresses. The Store scope can expose your own contact details if they’re personal — see Grant a user access . Orders modify can move money. With Orders set to modify, your agent can refund orders. A refund can’t be undone through the tool, so only grant modify to users who should be able to issue refunds. Scopes aren’t field-level. Each scope grants full read and write access across its area. For example, you can’t allow description edits while blocking price changes within Products. Scopes apply per user, not per agent. Every agent you connect under your account shares the same access. You can’t give two agents different scopes. No self-service view of connected agents. You can review and clear a user’s scope grant yourself, but there’s no visibility into which agents or sessions are actively using that access right now, and no way to force one off immediately. Contact BigCommerce support for that. Scope changes aren’t always immediate. When an administrator changes or removes your scopes, the change can take up to the remaining length of your current session to take effect. Sessions are kept short during early access to minimize this window. No agent attribution. Anything your agent does is recorded in your audit trail against the user who authorized it, the same as if that person had made the change by hand. Share feedback After you try Store Management MCP, send feedback from the control panel on what worked, what didn’t, and what you want your agent to do next: In the control panel, go to Settings → API and MCP → MCP . On the Management MCP card, select the Early access badge. Select Give feedback on Management MCP . Get help If anything is confusing, broken, or unexpected, contact BigCommerce support .

pages.title: MCP for B2B Ecommerce: Quotes, Approvals, and Pricing Rules (https://www.bigcommerce.com/articles/b2b-ecommerce/mcp-b2b-ecommerce/)
pages.text: MCP for B2B Ecommerce: Quotes, Approvals, and Pricing Rules MCP for B2B Ecommerce: Supporting Quotes, Pricing, Accounts, and Complex Orders Create your store and start selling today. Try for free Create your new website. See if the BigCommerce platform is a good fit for your business. Start your free trial No credit card required. Written by John Shieldsmith 11/19/2026 Share this article MCP for B2B Ecommerce: Supporting Quotes, Pricing, Accounts, and Complex Orders Get The Print Version Tired of scrolling? Download a PDF version for easier offline reading and sharing with coworkers. Download PDF A link to download the PDF will arrive in your inbox shortly. Key highlights MCP for B2B ecommerce is the use of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) so an AI agent can work with shopping lists and quotes for an authenticated business buyer, inside that buyer's permissions. BigCommerce's B2B Storefront tool set adds 12 shopping-list tools and 5 quote tools to the BigCommerce MCP server, and it's available now in early access (beta). Contract pricing, custom catalogs, company roles, and payment terms are set in B2B Edition, and sales reps still price every quote. The purchase order agent (currently in alpha) turns an uploaded or typed PO into a draft order on Stencil storefronts and is separate from the MCP server. Evaluators should pick one rep-less buyer group and pilot shopping-list approvals before agent-requested quotes. Driving operational efficiency with MCP for B2B ecommerce B2B isn’t always privy to the efficiencies that so often grace B2C. But, with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), they can be. MCP for B2B ecommerce allows agents to discover and call business system tools through a single interface. Best of all, with the MCP for B2B ecommerce, even complex B2B workflows can benefit from this agentic-driven model. There was a time when the question was whether AI agents would ever be able to help in the B2B space. Today, the question is now whether agents can request quotes for your accounts, route a restock list for approval, and hand it off to checkout without breaking pricing rules. With the MCP for B2B ecommerce, it can. Read on to learn how the MCP can turn Buyer Portal workflows , like shopping lists or quotes, into tools agents use to authenticate on a buyer’s behalf, what BigCommerce B2B MCP tools can do today, and how other platforms handle B2B in agentic channels. Psst. If you’re new to the protocol, read our developer guide to the Model Context Protocol , and check out our Storefront MCP launch post . What MCP is, and what changes when the buyer is an agent Within the ecommerce space, an MCP server is a service that publishes a store's actions, like searching products, building a cart, or requesting a quote, as tools an AI agent or AI assistant can find and use. Because the buyer can be an agent in this scenario, like ChatGPT or a third-party agent, it’s important the platform enforces every account rule, like custom pricing, catalog access, and so on. Which, the MCP and right ecommerce platform can do. MCP in one paragraph: servers, tools, and clients. The MCP client, either the agent or the app it runs in, first connects to an MCP server. It then asks which tools are available and calls them with structured inputs. Stewarded by the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation, MCP is capable of standardizing three things in its current specification : Tool discovery: An agent asks a server what it can do and gets back named tools and their inputs. Tool calls: The agent invokes those tools in one consistent format, with whatever system sits behind the server. Authorization: The protocol defines how a client proves it's allowed to act for a specific buyer. All of the above comes together to give B2B further access to agentic commerce , while allowing account-specific guardrails to stay in place. Which, again, is critical in the B2B space. Why B2B is a natural fit for agents. B2B commerce is rife with complex workflows : reorders, restock lists, quotes, and approvals. But unlike B2C, where customers are often browsing, B2B buying is often more of a task, and in many cases, a repeat task (like restocking in bulk). The repeat, rules-bound nature of B2B buying and its workflows make agents a natural fit. And, by embracing B2B agentic commerc e, you’re playing into modern preferences: 67% of B2B buyers would rather have a rep-free experience. What the MCP does not define. The MCP standardizes how an agent discovers and calls tools. It says nothing about contract pricing, account hierarchy, approval chains, purchase orders, net terms, punchout, or EDI. Those come from the platform behind the server, setting the guardrails that the agent must then follow. What BigCommerce's B2B MCP tools do BigCommerce has a number of B2B MCP tools that make it easier for businesses to embrace agentic commerce. Currently, BigCommerce’s B2B MCP set adds Buyer Portal tools on top of the catalog, cart, and checkout. Now, let’s take a closer look. One endpoint, two tool sets. BigCommerce B2C tools cover product search, carts, and the handoff at checkout. The BigCommerce B2B MCP tools cover different elements, as named in the develop documentation: Shopping-list tools: create_shopping_list, get_shopping_lists, get_shopping_list_details, update_shopping_list, delete_shopping_list, add_item_to_shopping_list, update_shopping_list_item, delete_shopping_list_item, submit_shopping_list_for_approval, approve_shopping_list, reject_shopping_list, and duplicate_shopping_list. Quote tools: get_quotes, request_quote, get_quote_details, send_quote_message, and generate_quote_checkout_url. Again, while seemingly not as fleshed out as the B2C offerings, the above are critical to B2B workflows and can save you and buyers precious time, enabling agentic commerce at the same time. How B2B tools are exposed to a session. The B2B tools will only show up in a session when the store has the BigCommerce B2B MCP integration turned on, and when the authenticated buyer holds the permission to access each tool. This prevents wrong prices or catalogs from being surfaced, and so on, while giving the agents the right access. Authentication itself runs through Storefront Session Sync, which passes a short-lived token at the start, removing the need for any login tool. Three quote tools (request_quote, get_quote_details, and send_quote_message) also make it possible for guests to benefit from the MCP, but only if the store allows guest quotes. Merchants can turn this on under: Settings Early access MCP Integration Configure Worth noting, each storefront will get its own MCP URL. For more on this, be sure to read our MCP server overview . Status at a glance. The BigCommerce B2B MCP tools are in various stages, with some being beta and others in an earlier, alpha stage. Refer to the below table to learn more about the purchase order agent, cascading price lists, and more. Feature Status Since BigCommerce MCP server Beta; enable via Settings → Early access Available to all stores since April 28, 2026 B2C Storefront tool set Beta; available now in early access May 11, 2026 B2B Storefront tool set (12 shopping-list tools, 5 quote tools) Beta; available now in early access [GA SWAP] September 16, 2026 Storefront Session Sync (logged-in shoppers and company buyers) Beta; part of the MCP server September 16, 2026 Purchase order agent (Purchase Order Skill) Alpha; Stencil storefronts only, Catalyst not supported Announced April 30, 2026 Cascading price lists Introduced at Commerce Live 2026 April 30, 2026 Pricing, catalogs, and company accounts: how agents work inside B2B Edition's rules The B2B rules that govern how AI agents interact with your store live in BigCommerce B2B Edition, not the MCP itself. This setup makes it possible for an agent to work inside specific rules as they apply to a buyer’s own session, as opposed to generalized rules. These rules, while varied and numerous, can be broken down across pricing, catalogs, and company accounts. Contract pricing: resolved by the platform, respected by the agent. Price lists and customer-group pricing are configured in BigCommerce. This makes it possible for a synced session to return whatever a company buyer's catalog and cart tools surface in the Buyer Portal. Quotes work differently: request_quote computes totals from base price and doesn't accept buyer-supplied pricing, discounts, or expiry dates. The sales rep applies the negotiated price, and the agent reads it back with get_quote_details. Cascading price lists, introduced at Commerce Live 2026, are also a platform-side setting that’s now available. Custom catalogs and what an agent can see. Company-specific catalogs are managed through B2B Edition's control panel and APIs. An agent's product search runs inside the synced session, meaning it sees the catalog the buyer already has. This prevents the buyer from seeing products and prices they shouldn’t. For more information on setup, be sure to check out the BigCommerce B2B ecommerce platform page. Company hierarchy, roles, and why the agent inherits them. Consumer-first channels take a different approach than those previously mentioned. Take Shopify's agentic storefronts documentation for instance, which states that B2B pricing doesn't display, while B2B-only products are excluded. That fits open surfaces, where shoppers aren't signed in to a company account. Meanwhile, on BigCommerce, company hierarchy, roles, and permissions are B2B Edition settings that decide which tools an agent can use. An approver's session gets approve_shopping_list, and a requester's doesn't. The agent can't do anything the buyer couldn't do in the Buyer Portal, and approvals still come from a person. All of this means buyers can still get the rep-free experience they want, you can benefit from more streamlined workflows, and pricing and catalog guardrails are respected. Look at the below table for a clearer illustration of what’s managed in BigCommerce B2B Edition, versus exercised by the agent through MCP tools. Managed in B2B Edition Exercised by the agent through MCP tools Price lists and customer-group pricing Catalog and cart tools return what the synced buyer would see Custom catalogs Product search within the synced session Company hierarchy, roles, and permissions Which shopping-list and quote tools appear in the session Quote pricing set by sales reps Quote requests at base price, messages to the rep, and reading back the offered price Payment terms, invoices, credit, and order-level approvals Not exposed through MCP tools Shopping lists and approval workflows through an agent Shopping lists are a core piece of the B2B buying process, while approval workflows ensure only the right people (or agents) have access to various products and prices. In BigCommerce, a shopping list has four statuses: draft, ready_for_approval, approved, and rejected. Lastly, a shopping list can also be deleted. No matter the status, an agent can build and route the list, letting people with the right permissions decide its outcome. What a company shopping list is. A company shopping list is a shared, company-scoped set of products and quantities. It goes through an approval workflow before buyers can use it to order. For distributors, duplicate_shopping_list is the tool to note, because it turns "duplicate last quarter's list" into a one-line request. The four-state approval workflow. The four-state approval workflow makes it possible for a buyer to do what they need to do, with the assistance of an agent, all while account permissions are respected. To better illustrate what this looks like, let’s imagine James, a maintenance buyer at a food processor who reorders the same safety supplies every quarter. Here's how his restock list moves: Kevin starts the list: He asks his agent to "duplicate last quarter's restock list," and duplicate_shopping_list creates a copy as a draft. He adjusts quantities: He asks to "add 24 cases of nitrile gloves," and the agent calls add_item_to_shopping_list. He submits it: "Submit my restock list for approval" triggers submit_shopping_list_for_approval, and the status moves to ready_for_approval. His manager decides: In the manager’s own session with approver permissions, he reviews the list and approves it with approve_shopping_list or sends it back with reject_shopping_list. Kevin places the order: The agent adds the approved items to her cart and hands him a checkout link to review and place the order. Buying can be a lengthy process, especially when everything is manual. The above workflow streamlines that, but without compromising on account permissions and access. What the agent can and cannot change. With BigCommerce, agents never set a list's status directly. The command create_shopping_list always creates a draft, and update_shopping_list keeps whatever status the list already has. Only submit_shopping_list_for_approval, approve_shopping_list, and reject_shopping_list move a list between states, but each still requires the right permission. Order-level approval at checkout is a separate B2B Edition workflow and isn't exposed through MCP tools. Quote-to-order: the agent-assisted workflow The quote-to-order process is another primary function in B2B, wherein the buyer asks for a price quote, the quote is accepted, and the quote becomes an order. Best of all, it can be assisted via agents, too. In an agent-assisted quote, the agent handles requests and follow-ups while the rep sets the price. This allows the agent to streamline things, while leaving the rep in control of the price itself. Here’s the typical quote-to-order flow, as assisted by an agent, with tools in parentheses: The buyer asks for a quote: The agent submits line items, one shipping address, and one billing address, priced from base price (request_quote). The rep prices it: The quote lands with sales staff in B2B Edition, who set the offered pricing and terms. The buyer follows up: Through the agent, the buyer checks status and can message the rep to clarify or negotiate (get_quotes, get_quote_details, send_quote_message). The buyer accepts: The agent creates a checkout link for the accepted quote (generate_quote_checkout_url). The order is created: The buyer completes B2B checkout , and the order is created in BigCommerce with a matching record in B2B Edition. With the right commerce data in place, like pricing and SKUs, the above workflow is seamless, delivering a less rep-intensive process. Which, again, saves your team time and offers buyers the kind of engagement they’re after in the age of agentic commerce. Why the sales rep stays the pricing authority. When the sales rep is the pricing authority, an agent can't invent a discount or expose another account's terms. AI agents, whether ChatGPT or Claude or your own custom AI assistant, exist to save time. But, it’s still important you have a human in the loop to ensure things are operating smoothly. By keeping a sales rep as the pricing authority, you’re doing exactly that. An added plus? This workflow matches how buyers are shopping today. As of 2026, 69% of B2B buyers still consult with a sales rep to confirm AI-generated outputs. What "complex" adds: addresses, messages, and multiple quotes. There are always going to be complex cases that arise in B2B buying. BigCommerce B2B MCP tools are still up for the task. The quote tools support: Per-line quantities Separate shipping and billing addresses Threaded rep messages Multiple open quotes per company They don't support multi-destination consignments on one quote, buyer-set pricing, or PO number carryover. But, with the above support, your buyers and reps alike can still save time and have a more streamlined experience. With guest quotes enabled, prospects without a company account can also request a quote and message a rep. The design is comparable to commercetools' Commerce MCP , which, per its documentation, scopes quotes, quote requests, and shopping lists to a customer or business unit and limits buyer-side quote actions to accept, decline, or renegotiate. Complex orders and the purchase order agent (alpha) Currently in alpha and created by BigCommerce’s Purchase Order Skill app, the purchase order agent can convert an uploaded or typed purchase order into a draft order the buyer can check out. But, this is only scratching the surface. What the purchase order agent does. The purchase order agent lives on a dedicated storefront page, where it waits for a buyer to trigger the following workflow: A buyer uploads a PO document or types a PO request in the agent's chat panel. The agent reads, interprets, and validates the PO document or request The agent generates a draft order that the buyer reviews. The buyer takes the draft order to checkout. Once again, the human in the loop stays in place. Nothing becomes an order until the buyer checks out, leaving them in the loop the whole time. Merchants also have the ability to add instructions, like pricing, order minimums, and payment terms , as well. Merchant teams get the benefit of productivity. With less re-keying of PO data, staff can spend more time on higher-value accounts. In the words of Joe Sharplin , head of ecommerce at AS Colour: “Automating purchase orders and improving how we manage pricing has been a significant unlock for our business. We’re reducing manual work, minimizing errors and delivering a more seamless buying experience for our customers.” Where it sits relative to MCP. The purchase order agent is a storefront agent built by BigCommerce, not an MCP tool set. Remember: MCP is the protocol that third-party agents use to call storefront tools. Together, they help turn a buyer's intent into an order. And while the purchase order agent reduces re-keying, complex orders still reconcile in your ERP. The agent doesn’t replace proper B2B ERP integration . Prerequisites and current limits. The purchase order agent is still in alpha, so its capabilities will grow over time. If you’re interested, take note of the following prerequisites and limits: Release stage: It's in alpha and installs through an alpha launch email. Storefront support: It works on Stencil storefronts only, and Catalyst isn't supported. File uploads: Uploaded POs can be up to 10 MB in supported file types. Quotes: An "Add all to quote" option exists, but the draft quote doesn't inherit the PO number or addresses by default. Be sure to read our in-depth documentation for a more detailed look at the purchase order agent and how you can utilize it. Where MCP fits alongside UCP, ACP, AP2, and your APIs There are more protocols than you can shake a stick at, including MCP. Understanding the differences is important, as each protocol has various responsibilities and uses. The MCP defines how an agent calls tools, as mentioned before. Meanwhile, the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) are both layers, defining how a transaction is expressed. Finally, the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), defines payment authorization. As of now, none of the protocols carry contract pricing, account hierarchy, approval chains, POs, or net-terms semantics. That's why authenticated, first-party MCP sessions are where B2B agent work happens for now. Protocol What it standardizes Status (dated) B2B semantics carried MCP How an agent discovers and calls tools 2026-07-28 specification is current (July 2026) None natively; inherited from the platform behind the server UCP How a transaction is expressed; can run over MCP Updated late August 2026, per McFadyen Digital (September 2026) None ACP How an agent-led checkout is expressed Remained in beta after its April 2026 release, per McFadyen Digital (September 2026) None AP2 How payment authorization is granted to an agent Moved to the FIDO Alliance in April 2026, per McFadyen Digital (September 2026) None REST and GraphQL: the system of record. B2B Edition's REST and GraphQL APIs remain the system of record for companies, price lists, invoices, and orders. Again, MCP is a layer agents use to act on that data, not a replacement for ERP or PIM integration. How other platforms handle B2B in agentic channels Agentic commerce is still relatively new in the grand scheme of things, so naturally platforms are developing their own ways of managing B2B in the space. Consumer-first surfaces, such as Shopify's agentic storefronts and Microsoft's Dynamics 365 Commerce MCP server , focus on shopper flows. commercetools and BigCommerce expose quotes and shopping lists to authenticated buyers through MCP. Salesforce runs its B2B Buyer Agent in its own channels, and SAP announced a storefront MCP at NRF 2026. For the broader picture, see the rise of agentic commerce platforms in 2026 . Platform Agentic surface B2B objects reachable by agent Status (dated) BigCommerce MCP server, B2B Storefront tool set Shopping lists with approval, quotes; gated per buyer permission Beta (September 2026) commercetools Commerce MCP Quotes, quote requests, shopping lists; scoped to customer or business unit Documented in tool reference (September 2026) Shopify Agentic storefronts None; B2B pricing not displayed, B2B-only products excluded Per Help Center (September 2026) Salesforce B2B Buyer Agent over WhatsApp and SMS Reorders with contract pricing, in a first-party channel Generally available per Salesforce (June 2026) Microsoft Dynamics 365 Commerce Commerce MCP server None documented; shopper flows only Preview (June 2026) Adobe Commerce B2B drop-in components No published connection to its MCP surface Undocumented, per McFadyen Digital (September 2026) When you’re evaluating various vendors , there’s one big question to ask: Which B2B objects can an authenticated agent reach, and who prices the quote? Evaluator checklist: Is your B2B stack agent-ready? It’s increasingly important that your B2B stack is agent-ready, especially with 61% of B2B buyers using AI in the purchasing process, and 38% using agentic AI in one form or another. Meanwhile, 90.7% of enterprises believe AI will influence 20% of orders, or more, by 2027. Determine whether your B2B stack is ready for agentic by scoring it against the following questions, with BigCommerce examples in parentheses. Data and catalog readiness. Base pricing: Is it accurate enough to be a sensible starting point for reps? Product details: Do names, specs, and units of measure match the words buyers actually use? Catalog assignments: Does each company see the right catalog today, since the agent sees the same one? Account and permission model. Roles: Are roles and permissions clean enough that an agent inherits the right tools? Approvers: Does every company using shopping lists have a named approver, so lists don't stall? Session handoff: Can your storefront pass a signed-in buyer's session to an agent (Storefront Session Sync)? Quote and approval process ownership. Quote response: Who prices agent-requested quotes, and how quickly, if volume rises? Rep messaging: Will reps answer quote message threads (send_quote_message) as promptly as they answer email? Guest quotes: Should prospects without accounts request quotes through an agent, and who handles them? Pilot scope and measurement. Cohort: Which long-tail, rep-less buyer group gets the pilot? Metric: Will you track quote cycle time or reorder completion, and have you set a baseline? Downstream fit: Do agent-assisted orders flow cleanly through your B2B order management and procurement processes ? For a first pilot with your B2B stack, start with shopping-list build-and-approve for a rep-less cohort, then add quote requests. Both keep a person approving or pricing quotes before anything becomes an order. The final word B2B ecommerce is perfect for the MCP because it’s heavily rules-based, and MCP allows those rules to stay in place. For proof, remember: BigCommerce B2B Edition maintains pricing, catalogs, and permissions, while your person in the loop approves anything before it becomes an order. None of this is hypothetical, either. The BigCommerce B2B MCP tools are available in early access. Take advantage of these powerful tools with just three steps: Turn it on in a test environment: Enable the MCP integration under Settings then Early access on a sandbox or staging storefront with B2B Edition, then confirm which tools appear for a requester versus an approver. Run two real cycles: Put one shopping-list approval and one quote request through an agent, with a real rep pricing the quote. Pick your cohort and metric: Choose the rep-less buyer group and one metric, quote cycle time or reorder completion, which you'll report on before widening the pilot. Ready to see it with your catalog and accounts? Talk to our B2B team today to set up a free demo. FAQs about MCP for B2B ecommerce What is MCP in B2B ecommerce? MCP for B2B ecommerce is the use of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for AI agents, to let an agent call a B2B storefront’s tools, such as shopping lists and quotes, on an authenticated buyer’s behalf. Pricing, account rules, and approvals stay in the commerce platform. Can an AI agent see my negotiated or contract pricing through MCP? An authenticated buyer's session inherits their account's pricing for catalog and cart tools, so the agent sees what that buyer would see in the Buyer Portal. Quote requests are submitted at base price, and the sales rep sets the offered price. Can an AI agent request a quote and turn it into an order? Yes, with a sales rep in the loop. An agent requests a quote with request_quote, the rep sets the offered price in B2B Edition, and once the buyer accepts, the agent creates a checkout link with generate_quote_checkout_url. How do approval workflows work when an agent builds a shopping list? Agent-built lists always start as draughts. A buyer with the right permission submits the list, and an approver approves or rejects it in their own session, using permission-gated tools. What is a purchase order agent, and is it the same as MCP? They're different products. The purchase order agent (in alpha) is a BigCommerce storefront agent that converts uploaded or typed POs into draught orders, supporting Stencil storefronts only at this time. MCP is the open protocol third-party agents use to call storefront tools. Is BigCommerce's B2B MCP generally available? Not yet. The B2B Storefront tool set launched September 16, 2026, and is available in early access (in beta). How is MCP different from UCP, ACP, and AP2? MCP defines how an AI agent discovers and calls a system’s tools. The Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) define how a transaction or agent-led checkout is expressed, and the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) defines how payment authorization is granted. They can be used together, and UCP can run over MCP. Do I need to build a custom MCP server for B2B? No. The BigCommerce MCP server (in beta) is hosted by BigCommerce, so you connect your agent to your store's MCP URL instead of building one. Setup details are in the MCP server overview. Which ecommerce platforms have an MCP server for B2B? BigCommerce does. Storefront MCP gives each storefront its own MCP server URL. On B2B Edition stores, it adds shopping-list and quote tools for authenticated buyers, gated by each buyer’s Buyer Portal permissions, on top of the catalog, cart, and checkout tools every store gets. BigCommerce offers a suite of APIs that let you manage store data, sign customers in, make client-side queries for product information, and write apps that integrate third-party services into store operations. BigCommerce API accounts play a role in every authenticated request to our servers. Our API accounts come in a few different flavors to meet the needs of different use cases. For example, app API accounts work well in multi-store contexts, whereas store API accounts are a good choice for frontend applications. Some endpoints only work with one kind of API account. For an overview of the authentication schemes that our APIs use, see the Authentication section below. API accounts BigCommerce offers three types of OAuth-based API accounts to developers who wish to use BigCommerce’s REST APIs: store-level credentials, app-level credentials, and account-level credentials. This section describes the difference between the three, how to obtain and revoke account credentials, and the use cases for each. It also contains a reference for available OAuth scopes and provides a compelling list of reasons to migrate from legacy API tokens to OAuth credentials. Every parent set of API credentials that you request for your store is its own API account . At its simplest, an API account consists of the following: The client_id uniquely identifies the app or user, or the client , making a request. The client_secret is a cryptographically secure value known only to the client and BigCommerce. Every active API account has at least one access_token . Store-level API accounts include a static access token that does not change. App-level API accounts expect each application to generate a unique access token for every store that installs the app. Account-level API accounts include a single access token that belongs to the parent account of the store that the user is signed in to at the time of creation. Guard these values closely. The client ID and client secret will never change; access tokens do not expire based on time and cannot be manually invalidated. It’s best practice to limit each account’s OAuth scope to only the privileges needed to complete that app or user’s designated tasks. Create separate API accounts for each app, store API user or function, or account-related implementation. Choosing the right kind of API account Where both types of API account are supported, review the preceding sections to make an informed choice about which best fits your use case. API or Use Case Store-level API account App-level API account Account-level API account GraphQL Account API , including Users × GraphQL Admin API × × GraphQL Storefront API × B2B REST Management API × REST Store Management APIs × × REST Storefront API × Customer Login API × Current Customer API × Payments API × × Apps that host REST Provider APIs (provider apps) × Apps that create App Extensions × Apps hosted in the store control panel (single-click apps) × Manual connection between a third-party app and a store × × Single-store frontend scripts × Store-level API accounts Merchants generate single-store API credentials when they create API accounts in their store control panel, in the Settings > Store-level API accounts menu. Use these credentials to read and change one store’s data with BigCommerce’s APIs. You can’t change store-level access tokens or OAuth scopes. In addition to the API account components in the preceding section, store-level API accounts contain the following attributes out of the box: An access_token , which accompanies most REST API requests. The client name is a label for your convenience, and it doesn’t accompany requests. The API path is the URL to which you make requests. The API path won’t change, but it will have /v3/ or /v2/ appended to it, depending on the current version for the endpoint you’re querying. Most APIs that work with store-level API accounts use the access_token to authenticate requests to BigCommerce. However, a few use the access token to generate a temporary credential. To learn more about special cases that involve store-level credentials, consult the documentation for the API you want to use. Be careful with client secrets Do not send your client_secret or access_token in plain text or an unencrypted payload. Be particularly careful with the client_secret . An attacker can use your client_secret to both sign and decrypt JWTs sent between you and BigCommerce. Creating store-level API credentials To create a store-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on Creating a Store API Account . Revoking store-level API credentials To revoke store-level API credentials, you must delete the corresponding store API account. If the client_id and client_secret are compromised, or the account has become unnecessary, secure your account by deleting the API account. You cannot recover a deleted API account, so take care. Delete carefully Deleting an account cannot be undone, so be sure before clicking the trash can icon. You can also use the checkboxes on the left side to delete multiple accounts at once – but be especially careful when using this option. To delete a store-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on Deleting a Store API Account . Don’t forget your webhooks and metafields Some resources are only accessible to the API account that created them. These include webhooks, metafields, and scripts. If you need to revoke a store-level API account, plan accordingly. Webhooks do not persist upon account deletion. Verify webhooks associated with an account before deleting it. App-level API accounts You can create app-level API accounts in the Developer Portal . After a store owner or authorized user installs and authorizes an app, most apps use access tokens generated from the API account’s client ID, client secret, and a temporary grant code to read and change store data. Generate access tokens with the BigCommerce-initiated grant code authorization flow. Some APIs use app-level API accounts to implement alternative authentication patterns. For a summary of all our authentication methods, see the authentication schemes described earlier in this article. For more on working with apps, see our Guide to Building Apps . The sections on Implementing OAuth and Callback Handlers are particularly relevant to generating access tokens. Creating app-level API credentials To create an app and its associated API account, consult our article on Managing Apps in the Developer Portal . App-level access tokens App-level API accounts do not come pre-configured with an access token. Each time a store installs your app, BigCommerce initiates a grant code authorization flow to help your app generate a dedicated access token for that store. For further details, see Authenticating an app . Revoking app-level API credentials There is no way to manually revoke or force-regenerate app-level API account access tokens. However, either of the following actions triggers a token refresh: When the store owner’s email address changes When you modify the app API account’s OAuth scopes After one of these changes, the store owner will be prompted to review the change and reauthorize the app the next time they click the app icon in the store control panel. Delete apps carefully When you delete an app in the Dev Portal , there is no way to recover the client ID or client secret. If you choose to do this, don’t forget to mitigate the potential loss of webhook and metafield -related data and functionality. To delete an app-level API account, consult our article on Managing Apps in the Developer Portal . Account-level API accounts Account-level API accounts are designed to work with the GraphQL Account API, which manages resources beyond the scope of a single store. For example, managing control panel users in the BigCommerce ecosystem. Current and future features available using the GraphQL Account API toolset allow developers to build custom integrations and solutions that require high-level access to store and platform resources. Using this API, you can integrate with third-party applications, streamline and automate business processes, and manage multiple merchant stores per account. Creating account-level credentials To create an account-level API account visit the account control panel or the store control panel for a member store at Settings > Account-level API accounts . To learn more about creating an account-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on API Accounts . When you create account-level credentials, they belong to the parent account for the store you’re signed in to. Account-level API credentials provide direct access to all the account’s stores, not just the store that was signed in at the time of creation. Their permissions are limited only by the OAuth scopes they were granted at the time of creation. Keep the access token and client secret secure. Revoking account-level API credentials An account-level access token is valid until the account is no longer active. However, you can manually delete account-level credentials. Deleting API accounts is risky and must be done with caution. Only users who have the correct permissions can perform this action. To delete an account-level API account, visit the account control panel and find the account you want to delete in the list. Click the three dots in the Action column, then click Delete . Follow any prompts that appear. Migrating from legacy to OAuth Legacy API Accounts BigCommerce no longer issues legacy API Accounts to new stores. Existing legacy API Accounts will continue to work until further notice. Migrate to OAuth as soon as possible. Benefits of migrating to OAuth We recommend migrating from legacy API credentials to OAuth, if you haven’t already. Migration provides a wealth of benefits, including the following: Unified requests : Send all OAuth requests to a single URL: https://api.bigcommerce.com . Using a common hostname prevents interruptions of service when a store’s domain or SSL/TLS certificate changes or expires. Latest and greatest APIs : BigCommerce’s V3 APIs are accessible exclusively with OAuth. Webhook subscriptions : OAuth API accounts can subscribe to real-time event notifications using BigCommerce’s webhooks. Shared secrets : Use new APIs and endpoints that require shared secrets, including the Customer Login and Current Customer APIs. Zippier responses : Responses to OAuth requests use gzip compression and less of your bandwidth. Better security with granular permissions : All OAuth tokens are scoped to specific operations and endpoints. If you suspect a breach, you will know which resources could be affected. How to migrate Before you update your API connections to use OAuth instead of legacy basic authentication, take the following actions: Create an API account appropriate to your use case. Keeping in mind the API endpoints your connections use, create either a store API account or an app API account per the preceding instructions. To adhere to industry-standard security practices, configure the account with the minimum OAuth scopes for your use case. If you’re using an app API account, you can always modify the scope later. If you use one of our client libraries , consult the library’s documentation for establishing an optimal OAuth configuration. After you create your connection, update your connection parameters as follows: Use https://api.bigcommerce.com as the gateway URL instead of the BigCommerce store’s secure hostname. For example, route requests that formerly went to https://store-{{store_hash}}.mybigcommerce.com/api/v2/orders/{{order_id}} or https://my-custom-store-domain.com/api/v2/orders/{{order_id}} will now use https://api.bigcommerce.com/stores/{{store_hash}}/v2/orders/{{order_id}} . Rewrite your HTTP request headers to use the X-Auth-Token header to pass the API account’s access_token instead of the Authorization header. For more information, see the access tokens section above. Rate limiting works differently for OAuth API connections. For details, see the Rate Limits section of our API best practices article. OAuth scopes Scope grants and limits a program’s ability to read and write data. Set the scopes to the minimum level of access your implementation needs. All OAuth scopes except default provide read-only permissions scopes so that you can limit some accounts to sending GET and HEAD requests. Webhooks are accessible from the default scope that is automatically accessible to all API accounts.
